readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: the coyote’s joke on Chink (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Decide whether an animal’s behaviour shows a “sense of humour,” or whether that is the writer’s interpretation.
readings.focus: A puppy sent to chase a coyote learns a hard lesson, and the joke goes on too long.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. In 1897 he stayed in Yellowstone National Park, where animals were protected from hunting. A picket-pin ground-squirrel sits up straight like a tent peg; to “lay for” someone is to wait to ambush him; tedious means tiresome.
readings.contentNote: The dog’s name, Chink, is also an ethnic slur against Chinese people; readers may prefer to say “the dog” when reading aloud. The writer hints that the dog’s owner secretly killed the coyote, although it was protected in the park.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “The Cute Coyote,” the section “The Coyote’s Sense of Humour,” whole; opens “To understand the Coyote fully one must remember that he is simply a wild dog, getting…”; closes “…it, but I have my suspicions, although in those days the Coyote was a protected animal.”.

questions.prompt: Why did Chink chase the coyote, and why does Seton say Chink did not get the sympathy he deserved?
facilitatorNotes: A camper told him to, “in a spirit of mischief.” Chink was only obeying, so the joke was really the camper’s, but everyone laughed at the dog.
evidence: in a spirit of mischief
after all he was merely carrying out orders

questions.prompt: How does Seton show that the coyote is faster, even though Chink seems to try harder?
facilitatorNotes: Chink makes magnificent bounds and war-whoops; the coyote slouches along, tail and legs tangling, and still has to slow down so as not to leave the puppy behind.
evidence: He doesn't seem to work hard but oh! how he does cover the prairie!
the Coyote obviously had to slack up to keep from running away altogether

questions.prompt: Seton says the coyote “seemed to be cracking a series of good jokes.” Is that what he saw, or how he explains it? What else might explain the chases?
facilitatorNotes: He saw chasing and nipping; “seemed” admits that the joke is his reading of it. The coyote might be playing, warning the dog off, or guarding its feeding place. Readers can weigh which fits best.
evidence: seemed to be cracking a series of good jokes at Chink's expense
The Coyote, however, had discovered a new amusement.

questions.prompt: What does Seton suspect happened to the coyote, and how does he tell us without saying it?
facilitatorNotes: The master grumbled that “something else would” happen, the coyote vanished, and Seton has “suspicions,” adding that coyotes were protected. He implies the master killed it, and the funny story ends sadly.
evidence: I'm not supposed to know any thing about it, but I have my suspicions
in those days the Coyote was a protected animal

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: a lost boy and a steel trap (the badger story, part 1)
readings.challenge: Follow two story lines that the writer will soon bring together.
readings.focus: Seton sets up a lost child and a mother badger who has lost everything.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. He says this story was told to him in Winnipeg, Canada, by people who knew the family; it happened in 1871. A Prairie Chicken is a kind of grouse; to barter is to trade; champed means bitten and chewed. Notice how Seton describes the neighbour, Grogan, before telling what he did.
readings.contentNote: A man traps two badgers: he clubs the father to death, and the trapped mother chews off a toe to escape, then finds her babies dead.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Old Silver-grizzle—The Badger,” the sections “The Story of the Kindly Badger” and “The Evil One,” whole; opens “But the most interesting case, and one which I might hesitate to reproduce but for the…”; closes “…next food, and then at evening she made for an old den she had used the fall before.”.

questions.prompt: What was unusual about Harry, and how did that habit get him lost?
facilitatorNotes: He copied animals’ voices and movements so exactly that people found it “uncanny.” Following a Prairie Chicken and copying her, he wandered until the house was out of sight.
evidence: imitating their voices and actions, with an exactness that onlookers sometimes declared to be uncanny
So he wandered on and on, till the house was hidden from view

questions.prompt: Why did the neighbours give up the search, and why did the parents keep on?
facilitatorNotes: The neighbours decided he had drowned in the river. His parents kept searching and praying “long after all hope seemed dead.”
evidence: believing that the child was drowned and carried away by the river
the parents continued their search even long after all hope seemed dead

questions.prompt: Which words show how Seton judges Grogan, and how he wants readers to see the badgers?
facilitatorNotes: He writes of Grogan’s “vicious cruelty” and “evil indulgence,” and gives the father badger “brave eyes” and a wish for “a fair fight.” He takes sides openly and tells the mother’s suffering from her point of view.
evidence: because of the man's vicious cruelty to the animals
The Badger craved only a fair fight

questions.prompt: Why does Seton tell so much about the mother badger before he goes back to Harry? Predict how the two stories will meet.
facilitatorNotes: She has lost her mate and her young and is heading for an old den on the prairie, where Harry is lost. Many readers will guess that she will find him.
evidence: her babies were dead
she made for an old den she had used the fall before

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: two weeks in a badger den (the badger story, part 2)
readings.challenge: Notice how a relationship changes over days, one step at a time.
readings.focus: A grieving mother badger feeds and shelters a lost boy, and he begins to live her life.
readings.context: Recap: seven-year-old Harry Service wandered away on the prairie near Winnipeg and was lost; neighbours gave up the search, but his parents kept on. Meanwhile a cruel neighbour, Grogan, trapped a pair of badgers: the father was killed, and the mother escaped with a missing toe to find her babies dead. Rose hips are the berries of wild roses; to slake thirst is to drink; to elude is to slip away from.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Old Silver-grizzle—The Badger,” the section “The Badger That Rescued the Boy,” whole; opens “And little Harry, meanwhile, where was he? That sunny afternoon in June he had wandered…”; closes “…men had passed near by, but the habit of eluding them was now in full possession of him.”.

questions.prompt: How does Harry know that this badger has been caught in a trap?
facilitatorNotes: She has five claws on one foot and four on the other, with fresh wounds. The reader knows from the last part which badger this is.
evidence: the visitor had five claws on one foot and four on the other, with recent wounds

questions.prompt: Trace how the badger behaves toward Harry from the first evening to the end of two weeks.
facilitatorNotes: She snarls and fights, then leaves him the den; she brings meat, sleeps beside him, sets an egg before him unbroken, licks his face; at last they play tag. Each step brings them closer.
evidence: I scratched the Badger's face and she scratched mine.
Sometimes they played tag on the prairie

questions.prompt: Why does Harry hide from the men who are searching for him?
facilitatorNotes: The first rider is Grogan, whom he dislikes, so he hides; after that, hiding becomes a habit he cannot break.
evidence: having once yielded to his shy impulse, he hid again each time
the habit of eluding them was now in full possession of him

questions.prompt: Seton says the badger’s “heart was yearning for something to love.” Could anyone observe that? Is it convincing?
facilitatorNotes: It is an explanation the parents worked out later from what they knew of her lost young. It fits her care for Harry, but no one can see into a badger’s heart. Readers can decide how far to trust it.
evidence: this was a mother Badger which had lost her brood and her heart was yearning for something to love

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: found (the badger story, part 3)
readings.challenge: Read a homecoming through all the senses, and notice what finally reaches the boy.
readings.focus: Harry is carried home half wild, and his mother’s voice brings him back.
readings.context: Recap: lost on the prairie, Harry sheltered in a badger’s den. The mother badger, whose own babies had died, fed him and slept beside him, and for two weeks he lived her life and hid from the searchers. Tow-topped means with very fair, almost white hair; a rebuff is a rejection; menaced means threatened.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Old Silver-grizzle—The Badger,” the sections “Finding the Lost One,” whole, and “Home Again,” to the boy’s tears; opens “One morning he wandered a little farther in search of water and was alarmed by a horseman…”; closes “…as the veil of a different life was rolled away, and he clung to his mother's bosom.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the horseman look twice at the den?
facilitatorNotes: He glimpses a whitish thing going down the hole, a strange yellow with none of a badger’s black marks, so he rides up quietly and waits.
evidence: the peculiar yellow of this and the absence of black marks gave it a strange appearance

questions.prompt: How does Harry act when his cousin, and then his father, try to reach him?
facilitatorNotes: He hisses and snarls, backs away, scratches and holds up his hands like claws. After two weeks he behaves like the badger, showing only “Fear and hate.”
evidence: The child hissed and snarled at him like a wild thing
menaced with hands held claw fashion

questions.prompt: In the long last paragraph, what does Harry hear, smell, see and feel at home? Which brings him back?
facilitatorNotes: The familiar room and pictures, the ticking clock, frying bacon, his sister’s voice, his father, and “above all” his mother’s arms, touch and voice. Seton names the mother first in importance; readers may argue that it is everything together.
evidence: the clock ticking as of old, and the smell of frying bacon
above all, his mother's arms about him

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: “My Badgie!” (the badger story, end)
readings.challenge: Weigh a writer’s claim that a strange story is true, and notice why he tells it.
readings.focus: The badger joins the family, is killed by the same cruel neighbour, and Seton asks readers to protect badgers.
readings.context: Recap: after two weeks in a badger’s den, Harry was found by his cousin and carried home snarling like a wild thing, until his mother’s arms and voice brought him back. Oscillated means swung back and forth; delirium is confused dreaming in an illness; extermination means being wiped out. Archbishop Matheson and the others named at the end were well-known people of Winnipeg.
readings.contentNote: A neighbour shoots the badger, which dies in the boy’s arms, and the boy falls ill with grief. Seton calls the killer a “halfbreed,” an insulting word for a person of mixed Indigenous and European descent; the slur reflects the writer’s prejudice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Old Silver-grizzle—The Badger,” from the badger at the door through the section “The Human Brute,” whole; opens “But even as she cooed to him, and stroked his brow and won him back again, there was a…”; closes “…you will join with me in loving him, and in seeking to save his race from extermination.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Harry’s mother stop the men from shooting the badger at the door?
facilitatorNotes: Harry runs to it crying “My Badgie!” and it purrs and licks his face. She sees it as a family would see a dog that had saved a child from drowning.
evidence: it was the mother's keener insight that saved it
as one might save a noble dog that had rescued a child from the water

questions.prompt: Why does Harry say he hates his father at first? Is his reason fair?
facilitatorNotes: He says his father passed him every day without looking. The father did ride past, but never saw him, and Harry himself was hiding. It is a child’s misunderstanding, though his hurt is real.
evidence: he passed me every day and would not look at me
the tow-topped head had escaped his eye

questions.prompt: Seton says he would “gladly leave untold” the badger’s death. Why do you think he tells it anyway?
facilitatorNotes: It is part of the true story as he heard it, it shows the cruelty he wants readers to oppose, and it leads to his last plea to save badgers. Some readers may wish he had left it out; others will feel the story needs it.
evidence: an incident took place that I would gladly leave untold
in seeking to save his race from extermination

questions.prompt: How does Seton try to convince readers that the story is true, and what does he admit?
facilitatorNotes: He names witnesses in Winnipeg, but admits they “may differ as to the details” and that the mother learned the story slowly, with parts unclear. The witnesses support the outline; the details may have changed in the telling.
evidence: These witnesses may differ as to the details
parts of it were far from clear

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: Molly Cottontail’s five photographs (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice how a narrator uses a trick, and ask whose side the story takes.
readings.focus: Seton uses a rabbit’s habit of freezing, and his camera, to save her life.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. In 1902 he camped with Sioux families beside the Cheyenne River in Dakota; the boys were hunting rabbits for supper. Rigid means stiff; “rattled” means flustered; drift logs are logs washed up by a river. Cameras then held only a few pictures of film at a time.
readings.contentNote: Seton calls the Sioux boys “redskins,” “little savages” and “Injuns,” words that were insulting then and are now. They show the writer’s prejudice; the boys were hunting for food, as their families had long done.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “The Rabbits and their Habits,” the section “Molly Cottontail, the Clever Freezer,” whole; opens “I have often had occasion to comment on the "freezing" of animals. When they are suddenly…”; closes “…log; she was safe in the pile of wood, where so far as I know she lived happy ever after.”.

questions.prompt: What does “freezing” mean, and why is Molly Cottontail especially good at it?
facilitatorNotes: Becoming perfectly stiff when startled until the danger passes. She is nervous, so a sudden sharp noise makes her stop, following the rule “Never rush when you are rattled.”
evidence: become perfectly rigid, and remain so until the danger is past
Never rush when you are rattled.

questions.prompt: How does Seton use a whistle and his camera to protect the rabbit?
facilitatorNotes: He asks the boys to wait for a photograph, freezes Molly with a shrill whistle, and does it five times, each time steering her toward the log pile. He hides his real purpose because he thinks the boys would not stop if he simply asked.
evidence: I knew I could not stop them by saying that
all the while steering Molly toward a great pile of drift logs

questions.prompt: Seton wanted to save the rabbit; the boys wanted supper. Was his trick fair to them? How do the names he calls them affect your answer?
facilitatorNotes: He decided for them that they “had enough game” and tricked them rather than asking. His insulting names show he did not treat them as equals. Readers may admire his kindness to the rabbit and still question how he treated the boys.
evidence: I thought they had enough game for supper
I cannot hold these little savages any longer

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: the poacher’s family (The Poacher and the Silver Fox, part 1)
readings.challenge: Decide how far to trust a story the writer heard second-hand, and follow a family’s run of bad luck.
readings.focus: Seton prepares to tell a poacher’s story, beginning with how a hard-working ranch family fell into debt.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. A Silver Fox is a rare black Red Fox whose fur was worth a fortune. Yellowstone National Park, mostly in Wyoming, was guarded by soldiers, and hunting there was forbidden, so killing an animal in the park was poaching. Gardiner and Livingston are towns in Montana, north of the park. A corral is a fenced pen for animals; alfalfa is a crop grown for animal feed; a travois is a frame of poles dragged behind a horse. A mortgage is a loan on a house: if it is not repaid, the bank can “foreclose” and take the house. The principal is the sum borrowed, and interest is the extra charged for borrowing. Unmitigated means complete; nefarious means wicked. A hired man’s wages in the story come to about $500 a year.
readings.contentNote: Josh’s father is badly hurt and later dies. Seton says he has heard the poacher’s rule spoken “by red men and white,” an old way of naming Native Americans.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Famous Fur-bearers,” from the last paragraph of “The Most Wonderful Fur in the World” into “The Poacher and the Silver Fox,” until the banker loses patience; opens “From a friend, connected with one of the Park hotels during the early '90's, I learned…”; closes “…though that must mean a wipe-out and would leave the fatherless family homeless.”.

questions.prompt: Before the story starts, Seton warns that names, places and dates are disguised. Why might he tell us this? How much of the story will you believe?
facilitatorNotes: He heard it from a friend, his informant may have mixed in details, and disguising names protects a lawbreaker. He invites us to question the details but insists the “backbone” is true. Readers can decide how much weight to give it.
evidence: the names of the persons and places are disguised
So that you are free to question much of the account, but the backbone of it is not open to doubt

questions.prompt: Why, according to Seton, do people feel “a sneaking sympathy with a poacher” but not with a burglar? Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: The poacher seems a daring good fellow, his life has danger and romance, and many people feel that wild animals belong to nobody until someone catches them. Students may agree, or point out that the law protects the animals for everyone.
evidence: How is it that all mankind has a sneaking sympathy with a poacher?
wild game belongs to no man till some one makes it his property by capture

questions.prompt: What does fourteen-year-old Josh do when he finds his father? Which act shows most clearly that he was “Western trained”?
facilitatorNotes: He wraps his father in his own clothes and the saddle blanket, rides for the neighbour, and builds a stretcher of poles to drag behind a horse. Making the travois needs the most practical knowledge.
evidence: He stripped himself of all spare clothing
Josh cut two long poles from the nearest timber and made a stretcher

questions.prompt: How did the Crees fall into debt? Is anyone to blame?
facilitatorNotes: The accident and death, a hired man’s wages and the loss of the cattle used up their money, and the unpaid interest made the debt grow. The banker is not cruel, only businesslike. It is hard luck rather than anyone’s wickedness, though readers may question a system that lets a family lose its home this way.
evidence: The banker was not a hard man, but he was in the business for the business.
it only made the principal larger

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: the tempter (The Poacher and the Silver Fox, part 2)
readings.challenge: Notice how a writer shows a character’s decision without saying it outright.
readings.focus: Josh sees a Silver Fox worth exactly what his family owes, and a dangerous idea takes hold of him.
readings.context: Recap: Josh Cree’s father was crippled in an accident on the range and died, and the family still owes the bank $500 on their small ranch near Yellowstone Park. Josh, now sixteen, works to keep the house, but the bank will take it in February. Hunting in the park is forbidden. A pelt is an animal’s skin with the fur on; a patrician is a nobleman; a quirt is a short riding whip, here decorated with beads and elk teeth; plaited means braided; “good medicine” means lucky; a .22 is a small rifle. Fort Yellowstone housed the soldiers who guarded the park, and the Canyon Hotel stood inside it. A stage is a coach carrying passengers and mail.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Famous Fur-bearers,” the section “The Poacher and the Silver Fox,” from Josh’s mail trip until his first weeks driving the stage; opens “Winter was coming on, work was scarce, and Josh went to Gardiner to see what he could get…”; closes “…of all was the chill thought at his heart that February 1st would see him homeless.”.

questions.prompt: Find two details that make the Silver Fox seem royal or magical.
facilitatorNotes: He is a size bigger, black as coal, with yellow diamond eyes and a frosting of silver like stars; the other foxes step aside for him as for a nobleman.
evidence: black as coal, with eyes like yellow diamonds
the other Foxes moved aside as the patrician rushed in impatient haste

questions.prompt: Why does the hotel man’s “five hundred” matter so much? What does Seton call the thought that enters Josh?
facilitatorNotes: It is exactly the sum of the mortgage. Seton calls the thought “the tempter,” as if something outside Josh were whispering to him, and it uses the poacher’s rule.
evidence: Oh, why did he say "five hundred," the exact sum
"Who owns wild beasts? The man that kills them," said the tempter

questions.prompt: Josh trades his treasured quirt for Jack Day’s rifle. Why does that look like a bad bargain, and why does he make it?
facilitatorNotes: The quirt is worth about ten dollars and is his lucky charm; the rifle is worth five. A month earlier he would have refused. Now he wants a gun, and readers can guess what for.
evidence: A ten-dollar quirt for a five-dollar rifle
A month before Josh would have scorned the offer.

questions.prompt: Seton never says that Josh has decided to shoot the fox. How does he let us know?
facilitatorNotes: Through the tempter’s words, the sudden rifle trade, Josh’s “half-formed plan” of going back to the Canyon, and his dampened hope when he hears that the fox is gone. The reader puts the clues together.
evidence: His half-formed plan of getting back to the Canyon was now frustrated
hope had been dampened

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: three sulphur spots (The Poacher and the Silver Fox, end)
readings.challenge: Make up your own mind about right and wrong in a story that does not settle it for you.
readings.focus: On a freezing night at Yancey’s, Josh waits in a hayloft for the Silver Fox.
readings.context: Recap: to save his family’s ranch from the bank, sixteen-year-old Josh Cree needs $500, exactly what a Silver Fox’s skin would fetch. He has traded his treasured quirt for a small rifle, although hunting in Yellowstone Park is forbidden, and now drives the winter stage through the park. Yancey’s was a roadhouse where travellers stopped for the night. Mountain Sheep, Blacktail and Elk are wild sheep and deer; the Moon of Snow is midwinter; a scout guided the soldiers. The sights are the marks on a gun used for aiming; Josh marks his with the heads of sulphur matches so that he can see them in the lantern light. Sorghum is a tall grass grown for syrup.
readings.contentNote: Josh shoots and kills the fox. He swears, though the words are not printed. The poacher’s rule is called “the Indians’ creed,” an old generalization about Native Americans.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Famous Fur-bearers,” the section “The Poacher and the Silver Fox,” from the fox on the hill behind Yancey’s to the end; opens “Small bands of Mountain Sheep he saw at times on the slope of Evarts, and a few…”; closes “…with the living lamps in the head of the Silver Fox. Yes! Josh was a poacher. Just once.”.

questions.prompt: Why are the soldiers and the scout at Yancey’s “still more dangerous” to Josh? How does he avoid suspicion?
facilitatorNotes: They guard the park’s animals and would arrest a poacher; a scout reads tracks and signs. Josh shows no reaction to the news, waits until everyone is in bed, and hangs his lantern where it cannot be seen from the house.
evidence: game guardians of the Park, and still more dangerous, a scout
Josh turned not an inch, he made no sound in response

questions.prompt: The first time the fox stands in the light, Josh cannot shoot. What stops him? Is it only the dim light and the cold?
facilitatorNotes: His sights vanish and the gun shakes like a stalk of sorghum. Seton blames the gloom and the freezing night, but readers may suspect nerves or conscience too; the story leaves room for both.
evidence: the gun was shaking like a sorghum stalk while the Gopher gnaws its root
cursed his own poor trembling hand

questions.prompt: After the shot Seton asks, “Who knows? Who cares?” and names the fur dealer, the banker and Josh’s mother. What is he suggesting?
facilitatorNotes: Nobody who gains from the fox asks how it died: the dealer has his prize, the banker his money, and the mother believes her prayers were answered. Some readers will hear quiet criticism; others will hear Seton excusing Josh.
evidence: Who knows? Who cares?
I only knew it would come, for I prayed and believed.

questions.prompt: The story ends, “Yes! Josh was a poacher. Just once.” Does Seton approve of what Josh did? Do you? Who pays the price?
facilitatorNotes: Seton calls the gun “fatal” and the fox a wonder, yet says the shot turned the family’s fortune and saved the house. He seems to understand Josh without quite approving. Students should weigh the family’s need, the law of the park and the fox itself, and may disagree.
evidence: he raised that fatal gun
It was the turn in their fortune's tide
Yes! Josh was a poacher. Just once.

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: the hoodoo elk (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Weigh a strange true story, and tell a writer’s joke from his real explanation.
readings.focus: A wild cow elk lets Seton photograph her, walk up and stroke her, and nobody can explain why.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. Yellowstone Lake is in Yellowstone National Park, where hunting is forbidden. An elk, or wapiti, is a large deer, and the female is called a cow. A hoodoo is something that seems bewitched or brings strange luck. Tom Newcomb was his guide. Seton numbered his photographs as he took them; the Plates were pictures printed in his book. Contraband words are forbidden ones: Tom is swearing.
readings.contentNote: Seton jokes that he is a “medicine man” with “Elk medicine,” borrowing Native American words for spiritual power.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Horns and Hoofs and Legs of Speed,” the section “The Hoodoo Cow,” whole; opens “One of the best summer ranges for Elk is near the southeast corner of the Yellowstone…”; closes “…the other way, and if you can explain the incident, you've got the field to yourself."”.

questions.prompt: Trace how Seton got closer to the elk. At what point did he realize something strange was happening?
facilitatorNotes: From a hundred yards in the woods he crawled to the sage at fifty and the grass at thirty; there he saw she was dozing in the sun, and stood up and waved Tom out. Then they walked to ten yards and even stroked her.
evidence: By crawling on my hands I was able to do this and got picture No. 2.
I was near enough to see that she was dozing in a sun-bath

questions.prompt: Seton tells Tom he is a “medicine man” who has hypnotized the elk. Does he mean it? How do you know?
facilitatorNotes: No: he is teasing Tom. He admits at the end that he only told her to lie down after he saw she was about to, and that he cannot explain any of it.
evidence: I told you I was a medicine man, perhaps you'll believe me now.
I didn't tell her to lie down till I saw she was going to do it

questions.prompt: Tom rules out three explanations. What are they, and can you think of one he missed?
facilitatorNotes: She was not sick (she was fat and hearty), not drugged, and not tame. Students might suggest that she was very old, deaf, unusually sleepy, or had never met people and did not fear them. Tom also stretches the distance from any house, which shows how amazed he is.
evidence: That wasn't a sick Elk; she was fat and hearty.
It wasn't a tame Elk, 'cause there ain't any

questions.prompt: Why tell a story that you cannot explain? Is a mystery worth telling?
facilitatorNotes: Seton has photographs to prove it happened, and he honestly leaves the puzzle open for readers. Some will find that satisfying; others will want an answer.
evidence: I had this curious adventure, that I shall not try to explain
if you can explain the incident, you've got the field to yourself

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: Bats in the Devil’s Kitchen (Chapter V)
readings.challenge: Notice how a writer’s strong likes and dislikes shape what he describes.
readings.focus: Seton hates holes in the ground and loves bats; in the Devil’s Kitchen, one feeling wins.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. In 1897 he spent a season in Yellowstone National Park, which is full of hot springs and geysers, places where hot water, steam or mud bursts out of the ground. The Devil’s Kitchen is a hot, narrow cave at Mammoth Hot Springs. A prejudice is a judgment made without knowing the facts; a prototype is a first model; abominable means hateful; noxious means harmful; antipathy is strong dislike; predilection is a liking; cuisine is cooking. A specimen here is an animal caught, and usually killed, to be studied. Long-eared bats are now known to live far north of Colorado, even in Canada.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Bats in the Devil’s Kitchen,” the whole chapter; opens “It is unfortunate that the average person has a deep prejudice against the Bat. Without…”; closes “…believe that the happiest nights of their lives were those spent in the Devil's Kitchen.”.

questions.prompt: Seton says people believe “absurd tales” about bats. What does he admire about them instead?
facilitatorNotes: He praises their brains, keen senses, fine fur and above all their flight, and compares them to the fairies of childhood. He does not list the tales; students may know some, such as that bats are blind or tangle in people’s hair, neither of which is true.
evidence: he accepts a lot of absurd tales about the winged one
equipped, above all, with the crowning glory of flight

questions.prompt: Seton’s journal describes the Mud Geyser as if the earth were being sick. Find two disgusting words. Why does he still say people are “fascinated”?
facilitatorNotes: Vomiting, spewed, gullet, retching and belching. Something revolting can still be hard to look away from, and his description works the same way on the reader.
evidence: this is the mouth with a severe fit of vomiting
All are disgusted by it, but all are fascinated.

questions.prompt: Why did Seton go down into the Devil’s Kitchen when he hates underground places?
facilitatorNotes: Someone told him bats lived there, and his love of bats beat his dislike of caves.
evidence: my ancient antipathy was routed by my later predilection
I was told that Bats "occurred" in the kitchen

questions.prompt: What surprised Seton about his bat, and what question did it leave him? What would you need to do to answer it?
facilitatorNotes: It was a long-eared bat, which he believed had never been found north of Colorado; he wondered whether these bats winter in the cave or fly south. Answering would take watching through the seasons. Later naturalists found long-eared bats much farther north, so his surprise also shows how little was then known.
evidence: a Southern species never before discovered north of Colorado
It will be interesting to know whether they winter here or go south

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: Bunny’s ride and the rabbit dance (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow an animal adventure told with humour, and decide what the writer really learned.
readings.focus: Seton carries a young Snowshoe Rabbit all day under his hat, and that night his captive drums up a crowd.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. Here he is riding with a pack train of horses in the western mountains. A wasps’ nest has just stung the horses into bolting, and Seton has thrown himself flat on the ground. The Snowshoe Rabbit, or Snowshoe Hare, has big hind feet for running on snow. A leatheroid box is made of stiff board like leather; a tattoo is a quick drumming; “ringing up central” meant making a telephone call, since calls once went through a central operator; an acetylene lantern burns a very bright gas; to disport is to play.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “The Rabbits and their Habits,” from the last paragraph of “The Terror of the Mountain Trails” through “The Rabbit Dance”; opens “It is good old wisdom to "lay low in case of doubt," and very low I lay there, waiting…”; closes “…for a social purpose, and is the only approach to a game that I ever heard of among them.”.

questions.prompt: Seton feels “a certain wild hunter instinct.” What does he do with the rabbit once he has caught it, and why?
facilitatorNotes: He decides at once not to kill it; he talks to it, realizes he wants its photograph, and carries it all day on his head under his hat.
evidence: Now I had him, what was I going to do with him--kill him? Certainly not.
I want to get your picture.

questions.prompt: How does the young rabbit in the box call the others? What does Seton think it is doing?
facilitatorNotes: It beats the side of the box like a drum, and Seton believes it is signalling to its friends, as if it were telephoning.
evidence: He was using the side of his box for a drum.
That little chap is ringing up central.

questions.prompt: Describe the rabbits in the lantern light. Why might they keep coming back after each alarm?
facilitatorNotes: They push closer and closer, one burns its nose, and an alarm thump scatters them, but they return and chase each other in circles. Seton calls it fascination; students might suggest curiosity, or that the bright light confused them.
evidence: pushing forward as though fascinated
reaching out to smell the lantern he burnt his nose

questions.prompt: Seton calls this “the only approach to a game” he ever knew among Snowshoe Hares. Was it a game, a gathering, or something else? What more would you need to know?
facilitatorNotes: He admits it happened only once and that he saw no other rabbits for weeks afterwards. The captive’s drumming or the lantern may have drawn them. One night is thin evidence, and good readers notice when a writer says so.
evidence: This incident is unique in my experience.
the only approach to a game that I ever heard of among them

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: the time I met a lion, and a worse peril (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice how a writer builds a joke by giving a listener the opposite of what he wants.
readings.focus: A reporter wants a tale of deadly danger from wild animals; Seton gives him a lion that did no harm and a cow that nearly did.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. The high Sierra are mountains in California; Mt. Tallac is near Lake Tahoe. A Mountain Lion is also called a cougar or puma. A thrill-monger hunts for exciting stories; to stampede is to run off in a panic; a halter is a rope for leading a horse; range-cattle wander freely on open land; a lariat is a lasso. “Ptomaine” was an old name for food poisoning, so the cowboy is joking about their canned food. A cow “in milk” has a calf and is producing milk.
readings.contentNote: The milk from the sick cow comes out streaked with blood and smelling foul.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, “Sneak-cats—Big and Small,” the sections “The Time I Met a Lion” and “In Peril of My Life,” whole; opens “A newspaper reporter asked me once for a story of terrible peril from our wild animals, a…”; closes “…where they washed it well, and back to camp, where we scalded it out several times.”.

questions.prompt: Seton tells the reporter that danger from wild animals is “practically non-existent.” What does the reporter want, and how does Seton disappoint him?
facilitatorNotes: He wants a tale of near death. Seton describes a lion that sniffed around the camp while they slept, then insists they were never in danger.
evidence: Danger from wild animals is practically non-existent in America to-day.
there can be no question, I think, that we were not

questions.prompt: How did Seton work out what happened in the night?
facilitatorNotes: The horses were gone, with broken halters and deep hoofprints; then he found a lion’s tracks around the beds. He reasoned that the lion came close to the horses and they panicked.
evidence: there were the prints of a huge Mountain Lion
inspired by terror of their most dreaded foe, they had broken all bonds

questions.prompt: How does Seton find a cow that is in milk? What does it show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He bleats like a calf in distress, and the cow that looks around but does not run away is the one. He learned this as a boy on a farm, and a naturalist’s knowledge of animal ways includes farm animals.
evidence: I put my hands up to my mouth and let off a long bleat like a calf in distress.
memories of boyhood days on the farm

questions.prompt: Why might Seton call the second story “In Peril of My Life”? Was he in danger?
facilitatorNotes: The title promises the reporter’s kind of thrill, but the “peril” is a kicking cow and diseased milk that the cowboys might have drunk. It mocks thrill-seeking stories; some readers may point out that bad milk can really make people ill.
evidence: I had nearly forgotten what looked like a hairbreadth escape.
Evidently that cow had been suffering from more than one milk malady.

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: bears behind the hotel (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice when a writer laughs at himself, and what that does to a story of danger.
readings.focus: Seton meets a mother black bear behind a hotel, then sits on a garbage pile to photograph a grizzly.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. In 1897 he spent a season in Yellowstone National Park. The park hotels then dumped their garbage in the forest, where bears came to feed and visitors came to watch. Today feeding bears, or leaving food where they can get it, is forbidden in the park, because bears that learn to eat people’s food become dangerous and often have to be killed. Alacrity means eager speed; an adage is an old saying; to snap is to take a photograph; the Plates are pictures printed in his book. Lives of the Hunted is another book by Seton, in which Johnny is a lame bear cub and Old Grumpy is another bear.
readings.contentNote: Seton goes very close to wild bears, which is dangerous and which park visitors must never do. He says mother bears spank their cubs.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, “Bears of High and Low Degree,” the sections “A Peep into Bear Family Life” and “The Day at the Garbage Pile”; opens “When we went to the Yellowstone in 1897 to spend the season studying wild animal life, we…”; closes “…XL, c. I was so calm and cool and collected that I quite forgot to focus the camera.”.

questions.prompt: What happens when Seton tries “the power of my magnetic eye” on the mother bear? What is he making fun of?
facilitatorNotes: She keeps coming. He is laughing at the old belief that a human stare can master a wild animal, and at himself for trying it.
evidence: turned on her all the power of my magnetic eye
apparently this old Bear had not, for she came on just the same

questions.prompt: How do the cubs obey their mother? What reason does Seton give, and how might he know?
facilitatorNotes: They race up the tree at one call and come down at another. He says mother bears spank disobedient cubs hard; his “I find” suggests he has seen or been told it, though he does not say how often.
evidence: like obedient children, they jumped as at the word of command
it is quite the usual thing, I find, for an old Blackbear to spank her little ones

questions.prompt: When the grizzly turns on him, Seton follows the saying “when you don't know a thing to do, don't do a thing.” Was that wise?
facilitatorNotes: Keeping still did not challenge the bear, and it went back to eating; running might have made it chase him. But the wiser choice would have been not to sit fifteen feet from a grizzly at all.
evidence: when you don't know a thing to do, don't do a thing
then calmly ignoring me he set about his feast

questions.prompt: Seton says he was “so calm and cool and collected” that he forgot to focus the camera. What does he really mean? Why end the story this way?
facilitatorNotes: He was frightened, and the blurred picture proves it. Ending with a joke against himself makes him seem honest and likeable rather than a boastful hero.
evidence: I had a dim vision of my sorrowing relatives developing the plate
I was so calm and cool and collected that I quite forgot to focus the camera.
